items.basis: The claimed mechanism of suppressing regenerative vibrations through spindle speed variation contradicts fundamental vibration theory, as increasing amplitude would typically excite more vibration modes rather than suppress them, as evidenced by [doi:10.4028/www.scientific.net/amm.192.185] on dynamic performance of machining center spindles.

The proposed solution only addresses thermal elongation during warmup cycles but ignores the critical boundary condition of steady-state operation where thermal gradients stabilize but bearing heat generation continues, as shown in [doi:10.1016/j.aasri.2012.06.032].

The candidate's own evidence bundle contains studies on thermal analysis of machine spindles that demonstrate thermal elongation is primarily a function of bearing temperature and material expansion coefficients, not spindle speed variation, contradicting the core mechanism.

The candidate fails to demonstrate any advantage over the baseline status quo, as thermal elongation occurs due to heat generation from friction, not regenerative vibrations, making the proposed intervention fundamentally misaligned with the actual failure mode.

Implementing controlled spindle speed variation during warmup cycles would require a sophisticated control system capable of precisely modulating speed while maintaining cutting performance, which is technically infeasible given the high spindle speeds and precision requirements.

The prediction of reducing tool center point displacement below 10 micrometers cannot be verified as the measurement system itself would be affected by thermal expansion of the measurement equipment, creating circular measurement logic as noted in thermal error studies.
